study.title: Hypothalamus and Amygdala Response to Acupuncture Stimuli in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
study.study_design: cross-sectional and longitudinal fMRI study with test-retest design; CTS patients compared to healthy controls at baseline, and CTS patients retested after 5 weeks of acupuncture therapy
study.blinding: subjects were acupuncture-naive and were not informed of a sham acupuncture condition, only that there would be 'different forms' of acupuncture during fMRI; subjects lay supine with eyes closed and vision of distal body regions blocked by volumetric head coil
study.population: Adults with Carpal Tunnel Syndrome and age- and gender-matched healthy controls
study.inclusion_criteria: CTS patients: pain and/or paresthesias for greater than 3 months in the median nerve distribution of the affected hand (digits 1 to 3, and the radial aspect of digit 4); Nerve Conduction Study (NCS) findings consistent with mild to moderate CTS. Mild CTS defined by delayed distal latency of median sensory nerve conduction across the wrist (>3.7ms and/or median-ulnar > 0.5ms) with normal motor nerve conduction. Moderate CTS defined by mild CTS and with delayed distal latency of median motor nerve conduction across the wrist (>4.2ms), but with normal motor amplitudes.
study.exclusion_criteria: Pregnancy; history of diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, thyroid dysfunction, wrist fracture or direct trauma to median nerve, atrophy of the thenar eminence, carpal tunnel surgery, current use of prescriptive opioid pain medications, psychiatric and neurological disorders, head trauma with loss of consciousness, or other serious cardiovascular, respiratory or renal illness; any contraindication to MRI (e.g. pacemaker) or acupuncture (e.g. anticoagulation therapy); severe CTS (prolonged median sensory and motor latencies with either absent sensory nerve action potentials and/or reduced (50%) median motor amplitudes); evidence on NCS of generalized peripheral neuropathy or localized ulnar nerve entrapment

conditions.scan_context: non-insertive cutaneous stimulation (tapping at 1Hz) at acupoint LI-4 using a 5.88 von Frey monofilament; same 7-minute block paradigm
conditions.tissue_level_reasoning: The condition description specifies 'non-insertive cutaneous stimulation (tapping at 1Hz) using a 5.88 von Frey monofilament' — the von Frey filament merely touches/taps the skin surface without penetrating it. Despite the condition_label saying 'sham acupuncture' and the penetration/depth fields referencing the active arm's parameters, the actual sham intervention involves no skin penetration. This is surface contact only, classifying as Level 3.

extraction_notes.note: Clinical outcome data (Boston CTS questionnaire scores, nerve conduction study values, grip strength values) are referenced as reported elsewhere (Audette et al. 2006; Napadow et al. 2006b) and are not provided numerically in this paper.
No adverse events section is present in the paper. It is unclear whether adverse events were systematically collected or simply not reported.

Coordinate space is labeled as 'Talairach' in the table headers, but the paper uses MNI space for normalization ('co-registered to standard MNI space'). This is a potential inconsistency; coordinates may be MNI-space coordinates labeled as Talairach, or may have been converted. This could not be resolved from the PDF.
No trial registration number is provided in the paper.

Expectancy was not formally assessed with a validated instrument. The paper notes subjects were acupuncture-naive and not informed of the sham condition, but no formal expectancy or credibility scale scores are reported.
Cluster sizes (number of voxels or mm3) are not reported for any of the neuroimaging contrasts in the tables.

The paper reports that sham acupuncture was always performed before verum acupuncture and order was not randomized for this reason. This introduces a potential order confound that the authors acknowledge but did not control for.

Table 1 includes a row for 'amACC (24)' at L −3, 13, 34 and a separate row for '(24)' at R 8, 26, 27 - the second entry does not have a region label in the first column of the table as printed. The brain region 'amACC' is inferred for the second row based on context and Brodmann area; this has been noted as ambiguous.

The paper states 10 CTS patients completed fMRI test-retest scanning and 9 HC subjects completed fMRI scanning; however, the cross-sectional analysis appears to use all available scans. The exact n for each contrast (baseline GROUP x STIM) is listed as 19 based on the total unique subjects (10 CTS + 9 HC), but this is an inference from the text.

The functional connectivity correlation between amygdala and hypothalamus (r=0.89, Bonferroni corrected) is reported as a within-subject correlation matrix across 13 brain regions. The Bonferroni correction was applied across the matrix. The exact number of pairwise comparisons in the 13-region matrix (78 pairs) means the Bonferroni threshold would be p<0.000641. The paper reports this as p<0.05 corrected - this has been preserved exactly as reported without further interpretation.
Conflict of interest statement is not present in the paper.

The paper does not report individual session duration for the clinical acupuncture treatment (only that electroacupuncture was 10 minutes, followed by manual needling at selected acupoints; total session length not specified).

DLPFC is listed in Table 1 cross-sectional interaction but is not labeled with a Brodmann area number in the table. Its description in the text as 'dorsolateral prefrontal cortex' and the coordinate (L −20, 49, 9) has been preserved as extracted.
Peak-only re-extraction: 0 contrasts updated, 3 new contrasts added
